The map above Elian’s desk showed every street in his city, every bridge and park, but it stopped at the river. Beyond its edge lay blank paper.

He had inherited the map from his grandfather, who claimed that blankness was not ignorance but invitation. Most people ignored it. They hurried through the city, noticing only traffic lights, shop signs, and the changing weather.

Elian wondered what his grandfather might have seen there, so one autumn evening he crossed the bridge and followed the river until the houses thinned into fields.

The silence arrived before the town did. Not merely quiet, but a heavy absence, as if sound itself had been carefully removed. Birds hung motionless in the sky. Leaves rested on the ground without trembling.

At the center of the empty place stood a woman tending a garden of glass flowers. She explained that the town had vanished long ago, and that its last wish was to be forgotten. But forgetting, she said, is not the same as disappearing. It is what makes room for new things.

Elian opened his notebook. He drew the blank field, the motionless birds, the glass garden, and the woman’s silver shoes. He did not write a name for the place. Some things, he decided, could remain invitations.

When he returned home, the river still ended the map, but the paper felt different. It seemed less like an absence and more like an open door. He would return there often, especially when he needed to.
